**What it offers**
- **An open recovery data index.** The site publishes the data behind its timelines: 72 measured pain points, 88 milestones and 73 cited sources across 15 orthopaedic procedures. The sources include 24 prospective cohorts, 13 meta-analyses, 11 retrospective cohorts, 4 registries, 4 society guidelines, plus smaller studies. ### Best overall if your surgeon/clinic uses one

### Best for self-tracking without clinic enrollment
- **Scar** — best for personal recovery journaling: pain, swelling, sleep, mood, meds, PT, and incision photo timelines. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/post-surgery-recovery-scar/id6791557397?utm_source=openai))
- **MoveAgain** — especially good for joint replacement recovery; includes symptom screens for complications and medication logging. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moveagain-knee-hip-recovery/id6761268590?utm_source=openai))
- **ScarTrack** — best if your main focus is scar/incision healing over months, reminders, photo comparison, and private on-device storage. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/scartrack-scar-recovery-log/id6781988879?utm_source=openai))

### Best if privacy and secure clinical photo sharing matter most

The most useful features are:
- **Daily symptom logs**: pain, swelling, redness, drainage, fever
- **Medication reminders/logging**

- If you mainly want **incision/scar photo tracking**, try **ScarTrack**.

The best way to judge your recovery is to compare it with your own surgeon's or physical therapist's protocol. What's "on track" depends a lot on what was done during the surgery. Below is a general guide.

## Typical timeline

- **Overall:** Recovery after a hip arthroscopy can take up to several months depending on which parts of the hip joint were operated on and your recovery goals. Full recovery generally takes three to six months, though patients with more complex labral repair or cartilage work may require additional rehabilitation time.
- **First 1–2 weeks:** Patients usually use crutches for one or two weeks after surgery and do six weeks of physical therapy. Some surgeons also recommend a brace. One practice uses one that limits the motion of the hip for the first four weeks.
- **Weeks 2–6:** Patients typically begin reducing their reliance on crutches as advised by their surgeon.
- **Weeks 6–12:** Many people need six to 12 weeks of physical therapy to help you regain strength and mobility in your hip and leg.
- **Return to sport:** University of Utah Health says it typically expect[s] recovery to take about four to six months before you are back to most sports. Another source says full sport can take up to 12 months.
- **Long term:** You will see continued improvements in your mobility and strength for up to two years after surgery.

## Signs you're on track

- You're meeting your PT's milestones: walking with fewer crutches or none, gaining range of motion, and getting stronger.
- Pain is slowly trending down over the weeks, even if some days are worse than others. Recovery is not always linear.
- Your activities are mostly comfortable. One guideline says any activities you participate in should be pain-free with the possibility of some soreness later. If you're sore for more than a day after an activity, you may be doing too much.

## Normal early symptoms

- Discomfort around the hip, lower back, buttock, knee, and ankle. The buttock, hip, and groin may become bruised and swollen.
- Fatigue, mild fever, nausea, and dizziness from the anesthesia or pain medications within a few days after surgery.
- You may also feel or hear fluid moving in your joint.
- Swelling should go down within a few days and the bruising will go away with time.

## Call your surgeon right away if you have:

- Pain in your calf, thigh, groin, or back of the knee. This can be a sign of a blood clot.
- Bleeding around the incision that soaks through the bandage.
- Tingling, numbness or weakness, a cold feeling or changes in color in your foot or toes.
- Pain does not improve after taking pain medication.
- Signs of infection: red streaks lead up from the incisions, pus drains from the incisions, you run a fever. Also watch for a bad smell or discoloration at the incisions.
- Severe or worsening hip pain, especially if it's getting worse instead of better over time.

## Things to bring up at your next appointment

If none of the urgent signs above apply, mention these at your follow-up rather than waiting it out:
- You've stopped making progress for several weeks.
- You still have a lot of groin pain, clicking, or catching after about 3 months.
- You can't come off crutches when your protocol says you should.

Doing your exercises consistently matters too: following your prescribed therapy program supports recovery. Your physical therapist is usually the best person to tell you whether your range of motion and strength are where they should be for your stage of recovery.

- research tools or study apps that collect pain data for clinicians/researchers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40412653/?utm_source=openai))

A key limitation is that a review of commercially available postoperative pain self-management apps found that available apps were generally **not scientifically evaluated** and lacked comprehensive evidence-based content. - surgery type
- anesthesia/nerve blocks
- age and health conditions
- pain scale used
- activity level at the time pain was measured
- medication regimen. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40412653/?utm_source=openai))

If your real goal is to know **whether your current pain is normal for your surgery**, the safest option is to compare it with your surgeon’s expected recovery pattern rather than an app. If pain is worsening, severe, or paired with fever, redness, drainage, shortness of breath, or inability to keep fluids down, you should contact your surgical team promptly.

rung.query: How can I compare my surgery recovery with published patient outcomes?

answer.answerText:
A practical way is to compare yourself on the **same outcomes, at the same time points, in a similar patient group**. Published surgical outcomes often use patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), plus objective outcomes like complications, readmission, reoperation, pain medication use, walking distance, return to work, and quality-of-life scores. PROMs are specifically recommended for setting recovery goals and benchmarking after surgery. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29293180/?utm_source=openai))

Here’s a simple framework:

1. **Define what “recovery” means for your surgery.**  
   Pick domains that matter for your procedure: pain, physical function, daily activities, sleep, wound healing, bowel/bladder function, emotional well-being, and return to work/sport. Recovery is best judged using both **objective measures** and **patient-reported measures**, not just one or the other. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30522719/?utm_source=openai))

2. **Use a validated measure if possible.**  
   Many papers use PROMIS, WHODAS 2.0, EQ-5D, SF-12/SF-36, or condition-specific tools for the joint/body part/disease involved. In perioperative care, experts recommend PROMIS or WHODAS 2.0 at follow-up such as 30 and 90 days after discharge. PROMIS scores are standardized to the U.S. general population with mean 50 and SD 10, which can help interpretation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29293180/?utm_source=openai))

3. **Match the study population to you.**  
   Compare only with studies that are close to your case: same operation, age range, diagnosis, elective vs emergency surgery, open vs minimally invasive approach, revision vs first surgery, and similar baseline health. Benchmarking guidance emphasizes that patient cohort selection and follow-up duration strongly affect whether comparisons are valid. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32398485/?utm_source=openai))

4. **Match the time point exactly.**  
   A result at 2 weeks is not comparable to a paper reporting outcomes at 6 weeks, 3 months, or 1 year. Surgical recovery changes over time, so the timing of measurement is critical. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/n/pcori420cer130601970/pdf/?utm_source=openai))

5. **Compare to baseline, not just to “normal.”**  
   The most meaningful question is often: “How far have I improved from my own pre-op state, and how does that change compare with published patients?” Guides to interpreting PRO studies stress distinguishing baseline status from postoperative status and understanding change over time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3340576/?utm_source=openai))

6. **Look for clinically meaningful change, not only statistical significance.**  
   In papers, a score difference can be statistically real but too small to matter in daily life. If available, look for terms like **MCID** (minimal clinically important difference), responder rate, or proportion reaching a functional milestone.

A simple worksheet you can use:

- **Surgery:** exact procedure  
- **Your baseline before surgery:** pain /10, walking distance, function, work status  
- **Your current time point:** e.g., 6 weeks after surgery  
- **Your current outcomes:** pain /10, meds, mobility, wound status, sleep, activity, complications  
- **Published paper outcome at same time point:** same measures  
- **Are patients similar to you?** yes/no  
- **Difference from baseline:** yours vs study average  
- **Bottom line:** better / similar / slower / unclear

Important cautions:

- Average published outcomes do **not** define what is normal for every individual.  
- Many studies report averages that can hide wide variation.  
- A slower recovery is not automatically a bad outcome if your baseline was worse or your surgery was more complex.  
- If you have red flags—fever, worsening pain, drainage, shortness of breath, new weakness, chest pain, calf swelling, or loss of function—use your surgeon’s advice urgently rather than benchmarking against papers.

One hip fracture study compared patients to the lower 25th percentile of normal age-matched populations.
- **Quality of life:** The EQ-5D-5L is used worldwide.
- **Specific procedures:** Many surgeries have their own tools, such as KOOS/Oxford Knee Score for knees, Oxford Hip Score/HOOS for hips, and BODY-Q for body contouring. The Royal College of Surgeons, for instance, recommends using the BODY-Q patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) to assess abdominoplasty results.

## 3. Find published results to compare against
- **PubMed or Google Scholar:** Search for your procedure name plus the questionnaire name, e.g., "total knee arthroplasty KOOS 6 weeks." Look for tables showing average scores at set time points.
